beats.narration_text: Here is what changed. Before AI: writing code was the constraint — humans spent most of their time producing lines. After AI: verification is the constraint — you get code in seconds but reviewing it for correctness, security, and fit takes the same time it always did. The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved.

beats.narration: Think of any production process as a pipeline with a single slowest stage. Goldratt called this the constraint. In software before 2023, the constraint was code production: engineers typed, syntax errored, debugged. That stage ran at human typing speed. The review stage — reading code for logic, edge cases, security — was fast by comparison because there wasn't much code to read. AI inverted this. Code production went to near-zero marginal cost. Review stayed expensive. You now have a factory floor where the input conveyor runs at 100× speed but the quality gate has the same one inspector.

beats.narration: Concrete consequence: code now wins whiteboard debates. Pre-AI you could argue for two sprints about architecture before writing a line. Post-AI, the faster move is to generate three competing implementations and run them. The one that works becomes the argument. This sounds good — and it mostly is — but it means your team's judgment muscle for speccing systems upfront atrophies. You get faster answers, but your ability to reason without generating degrades.

beats.narration: The CLAUDE.md file is the organizational tell. In AI-accelerated teams, the source of truth for how the org works lives in a markdown file that the model reads on every session. This is not a cute configuration trick — it means the org's working norms have become machine-readable instructions. When the file is wrong, every AI output inherits the error silently. There is no one to correct it at runtime. CLAUDE.md is load-bearing and almost nobody treats it that way.

props.code:
# CLAUDE.md
## Deploy process
- Run tests: npm test
- If green: push to staging
- Staging auto-promotes to prod after 30 min

## Code style
- No comments — code should be self-documenting
- Functions under 20 lines
props.caption: This file is your org's standing orders. If it says something wrong, every agent session inherits that error. Nobody reviews it on deploy.

beats.narration: The management layer flattens. In a verification-constrained world, the person who can read, run, and judge code is the value. That used to be a junior-to-mid skill; now it's the senior skill. Managers who can't read code become translators in a world where the model already speaks both languages. The teams that are adapting well have senior engineers staying as individual contributors — choosing not to manage — because their leverage is highest in the review seat, not the roadmap meeting.

beats.narration: The 'quietly stops working' failure. AI-accelerated teams have processes that depend on low code volume — PR review conventions, security audits, on-call rotation assumptions. These were designed when code landed once a week. Now code lands forty times a day. The process still runs, technically. But it's reviewing two percent of what it needs to review and nobody has reset the expectation. The failure is silent. Code ships. The audit log looks clean. The vulnerability lands in production without a ticket.

A small 'LGTM' stamp still fires at old cadence but covers only the first 2% of the bar. Final frame: vulnerability icon appears in the unreviewed gap. Label: 'Process ran. Audit passed. beats.narration: Before 2023, the constraint was code production. After 2023, it's verification — reading, running, and judging code that arrives in seconds. The management layer that spent careers reviewing code is now load-bearing in a new way. The 'quietly stops working' failure is the most dangerous: security audits and PR review conventions designed for low code volume, still running but failing silently.

beats.narration: Here is your turn. Open Claude Code and look at a pull request your team approved last week. Ask it: 'What assumptions does this code make that weren't verified?' Then count how many of those assumptions would have been caught if a senior engineer had spent an hour reviewing instead of twenty minutes. That gap is your verification bottleneck. That's the number to manage now.

Assumption 2: DB connection never times out — no retry logic
